newsitem.title: GERMANY: German gold revaluation plan finds few imitators.
newsitem.headline: German gold revaluation plan finds few imitators.

text.p: Germany's plan to revalue its gold reserves nearer market prices to help qualify for Europe's single currency found few imitators among its partners and some stinging criticism on Friday.
The central banks of Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden all told Reuters they had no plans to boost the book value of their bullion.

France, Italy and Belgium had no comment on the latest stop-gap measure German Finance Minister Theo Waigel found after an official tax estimate showed he would have 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less revenue this year than expected.

But there was some harsh criticism for Waigel's plan, which German newspapers lambasted as "witchcraft" and Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini warned could jeopardise the whole economic and monetary union (EMU).
A Reuters survey showed European central banks valued their gold in several different ways, few of them as conservatively as the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank.
The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price, a method which is normal under German book-keeping regulations.
The Bank of France revalues its gold every six months to reflect market prices while the Belgian and Danish central banks did the same annually.
The Dutch Central Bank adjusts the value of its reserves every three years, basing the new total on the lowest average market price for the period minus 30 percent.
A Bank of Portugal spokesman said: "It makes no sense to revalue our reserves as the accounting value is close to the market value."
The Belgian central bank has pioneered the sale of gold stocks, reducing its bullion from 1,300 tonnes in 1990 to 600 tonnes now.
The bank's last sale was in March 1996, when it sold 203 tonnes to an unspecified central bank, and central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse said in February no new sales were planned.

Italy, which Waigel once said would not join the first wave of EMU countries and most Germans would like to keep some distance from the euro launch, was quick to comment on what German critics were quick to call Bonn's "creative accounting."

"I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or a revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997," Dini told the International Herald Tribune.

"This would open up a wider gap than expected in 1998, thus making precarious the respect and sustainability of the stability pact. By doing this, Germany could put in jeopardy the healthy functioning of European monetary union," he warned.
A German currency expert slammed the plan as "cooking the books" and warned that the move could be unconstitutional.

Wilhelm Hankel, a former German economics and finance ministry adviser, told the Berliner Zeitung daily that if a listed company were to behave in the same way it would lose all credibility with the banks and its shareholders.

Waigel, faced with an 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall, said this week if gold reserves were revalued from current low book prices to levels close to the normal market price it could help solve the problem.

"This would be cooking the books. Any private company that manipulates its profit figures loses the confidence of the banks and its shares collapse. What the German government is planning is no different," Hankel said in an interview.
